extracted.intended_audience: law students, lawyers, and readers of English constitutional law and legal history
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and analysis of the nature, limits, and remedies concerning the royal prerogative under English common law, as set out in a classical legal treatise. Focuses on definitions, classifications, attributes of the sovereign, and remedies for subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monarch's duties under the original contract / coronation oath
rubrics_metrics.description: In the king's part of this original contract are expressed all the duties that a monarch can owe to his people; viz. to govern according to law: to execute judgment in mercy: and to maintain the established religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transcribed coronation oath text elaborates promises to maintain ancient rights and franchises, preserve peace of the church and people, do justice with discretion and mercy, grant laws and customs to tenure, and establish peace and order. These duties are fundamental expressed obligations of the sovereign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation of the king's prerogative by consent of the people / original contract
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the principal bulwarks of civil liberty is the limitation of the king's prerogative by bounds so certain and notorious, that it is impossible he should ever exceed them, without the consent of the people, or without violating the original contract between prince and subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text treats the limitation of prerogative as necessary to preserve natural liberties and maintain civil ones; it is a constitutional principle rather than an arbitrary restraint. Where constitution or law expressly limits prerogative, the crown must conform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and nature of prerogative
rubrics_metrics.description: By the word prerogative we usually understand that special pre-eminence, which the king hath, over and above all other persons, and out of the ordinary course of the common law, in right of his regal dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Etymology (prae + rogo) suggests something required or demanded before others; prerogative is singular, eccentrical, applies only to rights enjoyed by the king alone. Finch's maxim: 'the prerogative is that law in case of the king, which is law in no case of the subject.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between direct and incidental prerogatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Prerogatives are either direct or incidental: direct are positive substantial parts of the royal character (e.g., right of sending ambassadors, creating peers, making war or peace); incidental are exceptions in favour of the crown to general rules (e.g., no costs recovered against the king, king cannot be joint-tenant, king's debt preferred).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct prerogatives spring from the king's political person itself; incidental prerogatives relate to other rules of the community and are exceptions to them. Examples given clarify the two categories and indicate incidental prerogatives will be discussed in context of the rules they except from.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subdivision of substantive prerogatives: character, authority, income
rubrics_metrics.description: The substantive or direct prerogatives may be divided into three kinds: those that regard (1) the king's royal character, (2) his royal authority, and (3) his royal income.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These divisions secure reverence, obedience, and supply for government. The chapter focuses on character and authority (dignity and power); revenue (majora/minora regalia, fiscal rights) is treated separately as 'royal income' and linked to feudal distinctions between majora and minora regalia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royal dignity — sovereignty (king as supreme within dominions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The law ascribes to the king the attribute of sovereignty or pre-eminence: he is said to have imperial dignity; statutes declare the king to be supreme head of the realm in civil and ecclesiastical matters, inferior to no man upon earth, dependent on no man, accountable to no man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sovereignty explains legal immunities (no suit against the king) and the idea that no court has jurisdiction over him. The text contrasts English maxim 'rex debet esse sub lege' with Roman law justifications for despotic power and prefers the English principle that law makes the king.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royal perfection — 'the king can do no wrong' (twofold meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: The maxim that 'the king can do no wrong' means (1) whatever is exceptionable in public conduct is not imputed to the king personally or made him personally answerable, and (2) the prerogative extends not to do any injury; it is created for the benefit of the people and cannot be exerted to their prejudice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The doctrine preserves constitutional independence of the crown, and the law will instead attribute mistakes to deception of agents rather than to the king's intentional misconduct. Nonetheless, houses of parliament may remonstrate and ministers can be held to account where prerogative is abused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royal perpetuity — the king never dies (immediate vesting of kingship)
rubrics_metrics.description: The law ascribes to the king, in his political capacity, an absolute immortality: immediately upon the decease of the reigning prince his kingship is vested at once in his heir; there is no interregnum ('the king never dies').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal language treats natural death as 'demise' (transfer) of the crown; historical examples (Edward IV, temporary transfers) and consequences for process and continuity of government are cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royal immunity from suit and special legal maxims (e.g., nullum tempus occurrit regi)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of sovereignty, no suit or action can be brought against the king; 'Nullum tempus occurrit regi'—no delay or laches will bar the king's right; the king can have no negligence or stain (corruption of blood), and in law the king is not a minor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: property claims must be petitioned in chancery (a matter of grace), attainders purge on accession, statutes concerning rescission of acts made while underage discussed; these maxims support continuity and supremacy of the Crown in legal relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy for private claims against the Crown (petition to chancery)
rubrics_metrics.description: If any person has, in point of property, a just demand upon the king, he must petition him in his court of chancery, where his chancellor will administer right as a matter of grace, though not upon compulsion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This remedy is framed as equitable/petitionary rather than judicial compulsion; the law views such relief as proceeding upon natural equity and persuasion rather than municipal compulsion of the sovereign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies for public oppression: ministers, indictments, impeachment; limits of law against the sovereign
rubrics_metrics.description: For ordinary public oppression (not attacking vitals of constitution), the law provides remedies by examining and punishing evil counsellors and ministers, via indictments and parliamentary impeachments; the king himself, as sovereign, is deemed incapable of doing wrong and not amenable to ordinary judicial redress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where prerogative is abused to public detriment, Parliament can hold advisers to account; but where constitutional fundamentals are threatened, extraordinary remedies (e.g., abdication/vacancy, as in James II) may be invoked by the people or later generations. The law leaves some extreme cases outside stated rules, to be answered by necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extreme remedy precedent — abdication and vacancy when constitution subverted
rubrics_metrics.description: When a prince should endeavour to subvert the constitution, violate fundamental laws, or withdraw himself out of the kingdom, such conjunction of circumstances would amount to an abdication and render the throne vacant, authorizing a new settlement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Convention following James II is cited as a limited precedent; the text cautions that only the precise combination of circumstances in that precedent supports the remedy and that other imagined mixtures would not necessarily suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of absolute exercise of lawful prerogative and accountability of advisers
rubrics_metrics.description: In the exertion of lawful prerogative the king is and ought to be absolute—so far absolute that no legal authority can either delay or resist him—unless the constitution has expressly or by evident consequence laid down exceptions; if discretionary power is abused to the public detriment, ministers acting by his advice may be impeached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of prerogative actions listed (reject bills, make treaties, coin money, create peers, pardon offences). Distinction drawn between ordinary exercise of prerogative (irresistible) and extraordinary recourse to first principles when laws are inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royal exclusive competence in foreign affairs (king as nation's representative)
rubrics_metrics.description: With regard to foreign concerns, the king is the delegate or representative of his people: the king has the sole power of sending ambassadors and receiving ambassadors, and what is done by royal authority in foreign relations is the act of the whole nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explains the impracticality of collective individual subjects transacting with foreign states; unauthorized subject actions against foreign allies may be treasonous or penal (statute examples cited). Treaties made by the king may bind the nation, and ministers may be held to account if treaties prove pernicious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambassadorial rights, privileges, and limits under law of nations
rubrics_metrics.description: The rights, powers, duties, and privileges of ambassadors are determined by the law of nature and nations, not municipal constitution; ambassadors should be independent of municipal coercion and not subject to the private law of the resident state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an ambassador grossly offends, they may be sent home and accused before their sovereign, who must punish or avow them. There is dispute whether immunity extends to all crimes or excludes mala in se (e.g., murder). English law historically held that an ambassador loses privilege for offences against reason and nature (e.g., conspiring to kill the king could be punished).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity of royal grants procured by fraud or deception
rubrics_metrics.description: If the crown grants a franchise or privilege contrary to reason or prejudicial to the commonwealth or a private person, the law will not suppose the king meant an injurious action but will declare the king was deceived in his grant; such grant is rendered void on the foundation of fraud and deception by agents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law presumes the monarch's perfection; practical errors in grants are attributed to imposition by agents. This preserves royal dignity while allowing voiding of injurious grants when fraud is shown.
